title: Dividers, Couplers & Circulators
description: Split, combine, sample and steer microwave power: T-junctions, Wilkinson dividers, couplers, hybrids, circulators, isolators and attenuators.

study.title: The three-port dilemma
study.body:
A three-port cannot be **lossless, reciprocal and matched at all ports** at the same time (the S-matrix would have to be unitary, symmetric and zero on the diagonal, which is impossible). Every practical three-port gives one up:
- the lossless **T-junction** has unmatched outputs
- the **resistive divider** (three $Z_0/3$ resistors) is matched but loses half the power: each output gets −6 dB
- the **Wilkinson** divider is matched and lossless for the wanted signals, but dissipates in its resistor whatever is unbalanced
- the **circulator** is matched and lossless, but non-reciprocal.

study.title: The lossless T-junction
study.body: Two output lines $Z_1$ and $Z_2$ (each terminated in its own characteristic impedance) are simply in parallel at the junction. The input is matched when their parallel combination equals $Z_0$, and the power divides in proportion to the admittances: the lower-impedance arm gets more. Example: 66.7 Ω and 200 Ω arms on a 50 Ω line split 3 : 1. The outputs are not matched, and λ/4 transformers are needed to bring them back to $Z_0$.

study.title: The Wilkinson divider
study.body: Two λ/4 arms of $\sqrt{2}Z_0$ (70.7 Ω in a 50 Ω system) transform the two 50 Ω outputs to 100 Ω each, so their parallel combination matches the input. A resistor $2Z_0$ between the outputs carries no current when both outputs are driven equally from port 1, but it absorbs any signal entering one output, which **isolates** the outputs and matches them. Each output is −3 dB with a −90° phase shift. Unequal splits $P_3/P_2 = K^2$ use $Z_{03} = Z_0\sqrt{(1+K^2)/K^3}$, $Z_{02} = K^2Z_{03}$ and $R = Z_0(K + 1/K)$ (outputs loaded by $KZ_0$ and $Z_0/K$).

study.title: Directional couplers
study.body: A four-port that samples a wave travelling in one direction. Power enters port 1, most continues to the **through** port 2, a small sample leaves the **coupled** port 3 and ideally nothing reaches the **isolated** port 4. Coupling C says how small the sample is, directivity D how well the coupler tells forward from backward waves, isolation I = C + D. A lossless 20 dB coupler takes only 1 % from the main line: 0.044 dB through loss.
study.formula: \begin{aligned}& C = 10\log\frac{P_1}{P_3},\quad D = 10\log\frac{P_3}{P_4}\\ & I = 10\log\frac{P_1}{P_4} = C + D\\ & P_2 = P_1\left(1 - 10^{-C/10}\right)\end{aligned}

study.title: Directivity limits reflection measurements
study.body: A reflectometer measures the reflected wave with a backward-facing coupler. Because of finite directivity, a small part of the much larger forward wave leaks into the same port, with an unknown phase. Relative to the incident wave the error is $10^{-D/20}$, so the measured |Γ| lies anywhere between |Γ| − ε and |Γ| + ε. Example: D = 30 dB (ε = 0.032) and a true return loss of 20 dB (|Γ| = 0.1) can read from 17.6 dB to 23.3 dB. Measure good matches only with high-directivity couplers or a calibrated VNA.

study.title: 90° and 180° hybrids
study.body: Hybrids are 3 dB couplers. The **branch-line (90°) hybrid** has four λ/4 arms, two of $Z_0/\sqrt{2}$ (35.4 Ω) and two of $Z_0$: driving port 1 gives equal outputs at ports 2 and 3 that are **90° apart** (−90° and −180°), port 4 is isolated. The **rat-race (180°) hybrid** is a ring of $\sqrt{2}Z_0$, 1.5 λ around: driving the sum port Σ gives two equal **in-phase** outputs, driving the difference port Δ gives two equal outputs **180° apart**; Σ and Δ are isolated from each other. Uses: balanced amplifiers, balanced and image-reject mixers, antenna feeds.

study.title: Circulators and isolators
study.body: A magnetized ferrite makes a matched, lossless, **non-reciprocal** three-port: power entering port 1 leaves port 2, port 2 goes to port 3 and port 3 to port 1. With an antenna on port 2, a transmitter on port 1 and a receiver on port 3 it works as a duplexer. Terminate port 3 in a matched load and you get an **isolator**: forward loss typically 0.3–0.5 dB, reverse isolation 20–30 dB. It protects power amplifiers and oscillators from reflections (load pulling).

study.title: Attenuators (pads)
study.body: A matched resistive Π or T network reduces power by A dB and presents $Z_0$ at both ends. Because a reflection crosses the pad twice, a pad in front of a poorly matched load improves the return loss by **2A**: a cheap way to clean up a test setup, at the price of signal level. With $K = 10^{A/20}$, a Π pad uses two shunt resistors $R_1$ and one series resistor $R_2$; a 6 dB pad in 50 Ω is 150 Ω, 37.4 Ω, 150 Ω.
study.formula: \begin{aligned}& R_1 = Z_0\frac{K+1}{K-1},\quad R_2 = Z_0\frac{K^2-1}{2K}\\ & RL_{in} = RL_L + 2A\end{aligned}

steps.title: Splitting power
steps.body: A divider sends the power entering port 1 to ports 2 and 3. Ideally it is matched at every port and lossless, but a reciprocal three-port cannot be both lossless and matched everywhere. Each practical divider therefore makes a compromise: unmatched outputs, resistive loss, or a resistor that only absorbs unbalanced signals.

steps.prompt: A three-port can be lossless, reciprocal and matched at all three ports.
steps.explanation: False. With all $S_{ii} = 0$, symmetry and unitarity, the equations force at least two of $S_{12}$, $S_{13}$, $S_{23}$ to zero, which then breaks the unit-length condition of some column. Drop one requirement: allow loss (resistive or Wilkinson divider), mismatch (T-junction) or non-reciprocity (circulator).

steps.prompt: A lossless T-junction on a {{Z0}} Ω input line must split the power 1 : {{k}} between arm 2 and arm 3, with a matched input.

ask.prompt: What characteristic impedance must arm 2 have?
ask.explanation: Power divides as the admittances: $P_2 = P_{in}Z_0/Z_2$ must be 1/{{1+k}} of the input, so $Z_2 = Z_0(1+k)$ = {{Z0}} × {{1+k}} = **{{Z0*(1+k)|Ω}}**. Check: 1/$Z_2$ + 1/$Z_3$ = 1/{{Z0}}.

ask.prompt: What characteristic impedance must arm 3 have?
ask.explanation: Arm 3 takes {{k}}/{{1+k}} of the power: $Z_3 = Z_0(1+k)/k$ = **{{Z0*(1+k)/k|Ω}}**. With $Z_2$ = {{Z0*(1+k)|Ω}}, the parallel combination is {{par(Z0*(1+k), Z0*(1+k)/k)|Ω}} = $Z_0$, so the input is matched.

steps.prompt: {{P}} dBm enters a matched resistive three-port divider (three $Z_0/3$ resistors in a star). How much power leaves each output, in dBm?
steps.explanation: $|S_{21}| = |S_{31}| = 1/2$, so each output gets $|S_{21}|^2$ = 1/4 of the input power: −6.02 dB. Output: {{P}} − 6.02 = **{{P-6.02}} dBm**. Together the outputs carry only half the input power; the other half heats the resistors.

steps.title: The Wilkinson divider
steps.body: Two λ/4 arms of $\sqrt{2}Z_0$ turn the 50 Ω outputs into 100 Ω each, which in parallel match the input. A $2Z_0$ resistor between the outputs isolates them: it carries no current when the outputs are driven equally, and absorbs anything that enters a single output.

steps.prompt: Design an equal-split Wilkinson divider for a {{Z0}} Ω system at {{f|Hz}} in microstrip with $\varepsilon_{eff}$ = {{ee}} (for both line impedances, for simplicity).

ask.prompt: What characteristic impedance do the two arms need?
ask.explanation: Each arm must turn $Z_0$ into $2Z_0$ (two of those in parallel give $Z_0$): $Z_{arm} = \sqrt{Z_0\cdot 2Z_0} = \sqrt{2}Z_0$ = **{{sqrt(2)*Z0|Ω}}**.

ask.prompt: What resistor goes between the outputs?
ask.explanation: The isolation resistor is $R = 2Z_0$ = **{{2*Z0|Ω}}**.

ask.prompt: How long is each arm?
ask.explanation: Each arm is λ/4 on the strip: $\lambda$ = 3 × $10^8$ / ({{f|Hz}} × √{{ee}}) = {{3e8/(f*sqrt(ee))|m}}, so λ/4 = **{{3e8/(4*f*sqrt(ee))|m}}**.

steps.prompt: A signal enters **output** port 2 of an ideal equal-split Wilkinson divider while ports 1 and 3 are matched. Where does its power go?
options: Half to port 1, half into the resistor, nothing to port 3
Half to port 1, half to port 3
All of it into the resistor
steps.explanation: $S_{12} = -j/\sqrt{2}$, so half the power reaches port 1, and $S_{32} = 0$ (the outputs are isolated). The divider is matched at port 2 ($S_{22} = 0$), so nothing reflects: the remaining half is dissipated in the 2$Z_0$ resistor. This is the price of matching and isolating the outputs.

steps.prompt: A Wilkinson divider is used backwards as a combiner: two signals of {{P}} dBm each enter ports 2 and 3, with a phase difference of {{phi}}°. How much power leaves port 1, in dBm?
steps.explanation: $b_1 = \frac{-j}{\sqrt{2}}(a_2 + a_3)$, so $|b_1|^2 = \frac{1}{2}|a_2 + a_3|^2 = P(1 + \cos\varphi)$ for equal amplitudes. 1 + cos {{phi}}° = {{1+cos(rad(phi))}}, so $P_1$ = {{P}} + 10 log({{1+cos(rad(phi))}}) = **{{P+10*log10(1+cos(rad(phi)))}} dBm**. The rest, $P(1 - \cos\varphi)$, heats the resistor; in phase, the two signals add to +3 dB.

steps.prompt: Two equal signals of {{P}} dBm drive the outputs of a Wilkinson combiner. The green curve is the combined power at port 1, the orange curve the power burnt in the resistor, both versus the phase difference φ. Drag φ until port 1 delivers {{T}} dBm.
steps.explanation: Port 1 gets $P(1 + \cos\varphi)$. For {{T}} dBm: 1 + cos φ = $10^{({{T}} - {{P}})/10}$ = {{10^(d/10)}}, so φ = arccos({{10^(d/10)-1}}) = **{{pt}}°**. The remaining $P(1 - \cos\varphi)$ goes into the resistor, so in milliwatts the two curves always add up to the total input, {{P+3.01}} dBm.

steps.title: Coupling, directivity, isolation
steps.body: Port 1 is the input, port 2 the through port, port 3 the coupled port and port 4 the isolated port. Coupling C: how far the sample is below the input. Directivity D: how far the leakage at the isolated port is below the sample. Isolation I = C + D.

steps.prompt: {{P1}} dBm enters port 1 of a lossless directional coupler with C = {{C}} dB and D = {{D}} dB; all other ports are matched.

ask.prompt: How much power leaves the coupled port, in dBm?
How much power leaks out of the isolated port, in dBm?
ask.explanation: The isolation is I = C + D = {{C+D}} dB, so $P_4$ = {{P1}} − {{C+D}} = **{{P1-C-D}} dBm**.

ask.prompt: How much power continues to the through port, in dBm?
ask.explanation: The coupler takes $10^{-C/10}$ = {{10^(-C/10)}} of the power (the leakage to port 4 is negligible). Lossless: $P_2 = P_1(1 - 10^{-C/10})$, i.e. {{P1}} + 10 log({{1-10^(-C/10)}}) = **{{P1+10*log10(1-10^(-C/10))}} dBm**.

steps.prompt: Match each port of a directional coupler (driven at port 1) to its role.
steps.explanation: The wave travelling from port 1 continues to port 2 and couples into port 3. A wave travelling the other way (from port 2) would couple into port 4 instead; that is what makes the coupler directional.

steps.title: Directivity and reflection measurements
steps.body: To measure a reflection, sample the backward wave with a coupler. Finite directivity lets a fraction $\varepsilon = 10^{-D/20}$ of the forward wave leak into the same port with an unknown phase, so the reading lies between |Γ| − ε and |Γ| + ε.

steps.prompt: A load with a true return loss of {{RL}} dB is measured with a reflectometer whose coupler has {{D}} dB directivity.

ask.prompt: What is the lowest return loss the meter could show?
ask.explanation: |Γ| = $10^{-RL/20}$ = {{G}}, ε = $10^{-D/20}$ = {{eps}}. Worst case the leakage adds in phase: {{G+eps}}, i.e. RL = **{{-20*log10(G+eps)}} dB**.

ask.prompt: What is the highest return loss the meter could show?
ask.explanation: |Γ| = {{G}}, ε = {{eps}}. If the leakage is in antiphase: {{G-eps}}, i.e. RL = **{{-20*log10(G-eps)}} dB**: the load looks better than it is.

steps.title: Hybrids
steps.body: A hybrid is a 3 dB coupler: the input splits equally. In the branch-line (90°) hybrid the two outputs are 90° apart; in the rat-race (180°) hybrid they are in phase when fed from the Σ port and 180° apart when fed from the Δ port. In both, one port stays isolated.

steps.prompt: What comes out of an ideal branch-line (90°) hybrid driven at port 1?
options: Equal halves (−3 dB) at ports 2 and 3, 90° apart; nothing at port 4
Equal halves at ports 2 and 3, in phase
Equal halves at ports 2 and 3, 180° apart
A quarter of the power (−6 dB) at each of ports 2, 3 and 4
steps.explanation: From the S-matrix: $S_{21} = -j/\sqrt{2}$ (−90°), $S_{31} = -1/\sqrt{2}$ (−180°), $S_{41} = 0$. Both outputs carry half the power and differ by 90°. In-phase or 180° outputs are what a rat-race hybrid gives.

steps.prompt: What characteristic impedance do the two series (through) arms of a branch-line hybrid for {{Z0}} Ω need?
steps.explanation: The through arms are $Z_0/\sqrt{2}$ = {{Z0}}/1.414 = **{{Z0/sqrt(2)|Ω}}**; the two shunt arms are {{Z0}} Ω. All four arms are λ/4 long at the centre frequency.

steps.prompt: Feeding the Δ port of a rat-race hybrid gives two equal outputs 180° apart, and nothing comes out of the Σ port.
steps.explanation: True. The ring paths from the Δ port to the two outputs differ by λ/2, so the outputs are in antiphase, and the two paths to the Σ port cancel. Used backwards, the same hybrid delivers the sum of two inputs at Σ and their difference at Δ.

steps.prompt: A circulator passes power 1 → 2 → 3 → 1. A signal enters port {{p}}. Where does it leave?
steps.explanation: Follow the arrow: port 1 goes to 2, port 2 to 3, port 3 back to 1. So a signal entering port {{p}} leaves port **{{mod(p,3)+1}}**. Nothing goes against the arrow (ideally).

steps.prompt: A {{P}} dBm power amplifier drives an antenna with VSWR {{S}} through an isolator with {{IL}} dB insertion loss and {{I}} dB isolation.

ask.prompt: How much reflected power gets back to the amplifier, in dBm?
ask.explanation: Forward through the isolator: {{P}} − {{IL}} = {{P-IL}} dBm reaches the antenna. |Γ| = ({{S}} − 1)/({{S}} + 1) = {{G}}, so {{20*log10(G)}} dB of that reflects: {{P-IL+20*log10(G)}} dBm. The isolator lets only −{{I}} dB of it through backward: **{{P-IL+20*log10(G)-I}} dBm** at the amplifier.

ask.prompt: How much power does the isolator's internal load absorb, in dBm?
ask.explanation: The reflected wave, {{P}} − {{IL}} + 20 log({{G}}) = **{{P-IL+20*log10(G)}} dBm**, is steered by the circulator into the load on its third port (neglecting the small reverse loss). That load must be rated for it.

steps.prompt: Design a matched Π attenuator of {{A}} dB for a {{Z0}} Ω system.

ask.prompt: Find the shunt resistors $R_1$.
Find the series resistor $R_2$.

steps.prompt: A source with open-circuit voltage {{Vs|V}} and 50 Ω internal resistance drives a 50 Ω load through a matched {{A}} dB Π pad ($R_1$ = {{R1|Ω}}, $R_2$ = {{R2|Ω}}). Find the voltage across the load.
steps.explanation: The pad is matched, so the source sees 50 Ω and the pad input sits at $V_s/2$ = {{Vs/2|V}}. The pad divides the voltage by $K = 10^{A/20}$ = {{K}}: $V_L$ = {{Vs/2|V}} / {{K}} = **{{abs(V_RL)|V}}**. (Power: {{A}} dB less than the {{(Vs/2)^2/50|W}} a direct connection would deliver.)

steps.prompt: A badly matched load has a return loss of {{RLL}} dB. You put a matched {{A}} dB pad in front of it. What VSWR does the source now see?
steps.explanation: The reflection passes the pad twice: RL = {{RLL}} + 2 × {{A}} = {{RLL+2*A}} dB, so |Γ| = {{G}} and VSWR = (1 + {{G}})/(1 − {{G}}) = **{{(1+G)/(1-G)}}** (the load alone: {{(1+10^(-RLL/20))/(1-10^(-RLL/20))}}). The price: {{A}} dB less power at the load.

steps.prompt: To monitor a {{P}} dBm transmitter, a {{C}} dB directional coupler feeds a power meter through a {{A}} dB attenuator. What does the meter read, in dBm?
steps.explanation: Losses in dB simply add: {{P}} − {{C}} − {{A}} = **{{P-C-A}} dBm**. The coupler takes only $10^{-C/10}$ of the power, so the transmitter barely notices.

steps.prompt: Match each component to its key property.
pairs: Matched, but −6 dB to each output
steps.explanation: Each three-port gives up one ideal: the T-junction its output match, the resistive divider half its power, the Wilkinson only unbalanced power (in its resistor), the circulator reciprocity.

steps.prompt: Replacing an isolator in front of an oscillator by a 10 dB attenuator gives the same protection against load changes without any drawback.
steps.explanation: False. The pad does reduce what reflects back by 2 × 10 = 20 dB, about what an isolator achieves, but it also throws away 90 % (10 dB) of the forward power. An isolator gives 20–30 dB of reverse isolation for only 0.3–0.5 dB of forward loss.

steps.prompt: Design an unequal Wilkinson divider for 50 Ω with $P_3/P_2 = K^2$ = {{r}}. Use $Z_{03} = Z_0\sqrt{(1+K^2)/K^3}$, $Z_{02} = K^2Z_{03}$ and $R = Z_0(K + 1/K)$ (outputs loaded by $KZ_0$ and $Z_0/K$).

ask.explanation: $Z_{03}$ = {{50*sqrt((1+K^2)/K^3)|Ω}}, so $Z_{02} = K^2Z_{03}$ = {{r}} × {{50*sqrt((1+K^2)/K^3)}} = **{{r*50*sqrt((1+K^2)/K^3)|Ω}}**. The arm feeding the weaker output has the higher impedance.

ask.prompt: Find the isolation resistor $R$.

steps.prompt: A balanced amplifier uses two identical amplifiers between two 90° hybrids. Each amplifier input has $|\Gamma_A|$ = {{G}}. {{P}} dBm drives the input hybrid.

ask.prompt: What $|\Gamma_{in}|$ does the source see (ideal hybrids)?
ask.explanation: One reflection travels the hybrid's −90° path twice (−180° in total), the other its −180° path twice (−360°). At the input port they arrive 180° apart and cancel: $|\Gamma_{in}|$ = **0** for any $|\Gamma_A|$, here {{G}} (in practice limited by hybrid imbalance). At the isolated port both arrive with −270° and add.

ask.prompt: How much power ends up in the termination of the input hybrid's isolated port, in dBm?
ask.explanation: All reflected power, $|\Gamma_A|^2$ of the input, is steered to the isolated port: {{P}} + 20 log({{G}}) = **{{P+20*log10(G)}} dBm**. That is why balanced amplifiers give a good input match even with mismatched (e.g. noise-matched) transistors.

steps.prompt: Two signals of {{P}} dBm each, {{phi}}° apart in phase, enter the two outputs of a rat-race hybrid (used as a combiner).

ask.prompt: How much power leaves the Σ port, in dBm?
ask.explanation: Σ sums the inputs: $|b_\Sigma|^2 = \frac{1}{2}|a_2 + a_3|^2 = P(1 + \cos\varphi)$. 1 + cos {{phi}}° = {{1+cos(rad(phi))}}: {{P}} + 10 log({{1+cos(rad(phi))}}) = **{{P+10*log10(1+cos(rad(phi)))}} dBm**.

ask.prompt: How much power leaves the Δ port, in dBm?
ask.explanation: Δ takes the difference: $P(1 - \cos\varphi)$. 1 − cos {{phi}}° = {{1-cos(rad(phi))}}: {{P}} + 10 log({{1-cos(rad(phi))}}) = **{{P+10*log10(1-cos(rad(phi)))}} dBm**. Monopulse radars use exactly this to find the direction of a target.

steps.prompt: A lossless T-junction splits a 50 Ω line into arms of $Z_2$ = {{Z2|Ω}} and $Z_3$ = {{Z3|Ω}}. Looking back into the junction from arm 2 (input and arm 3 terminated in their own $Z_0$), what is $|\Gamma|$?
steps.explanation: From arm 2 you see the input line and arm 3 in parallel: 50 ∥ {{Z3}} = {{Zs|Ω}}. On a {{Z2|Ω}} line: |Γ| = |{{Zs}} − {{Z2}}| / ({{Zs}} + {{Z2}}) = **{{abs(Zs-Z2)/(Zs+Z2)}}**. That is the unmatched output of the lossless T.

steps.prompt: A circulator is used as a duplexer: transmitter ({{P}} dBm) on port 1, antenna on port 2, receiver on port 3. It has {{IL}} dB insertion loss and {{I}} dB isolation; the antenna has VSWR {{S}}.

ask.prompt: How much transmitter power leaks directly from port 1 to the receiver, in dBm?
ask.explanation: Port 1 → port 3 is the reverse direction, attenuated by the isolation: {{P}} − {{I}} = **{{P-I}} dBm**.

ask.prompt: How much transmitter power reaches the receiver via the antenna reflection, in dBm?
ask.explanation: To the antenna: −{{IL}} dB; reflection |Γ| = {{G}}: {{20*log10(G)}} dB; back through the circulator in the forward direction 2 → 3: −{{IL}} dB. Total: {{P}} − {{2*IL}} + ({{20*log10(G)}}) = **{{P-2*IL+20*log10(G)}} dBm**, compared with {{P-I}} dBm of direct leakage. The antenna match often limits TX–RX isolation.

steps.prompt: In a balanced amplifier, if one of the two amplifiers fails completely, the output power drops by 6 dB.
steps.explanation: True. The input hybrid sends half the power to each amplifier. With one dead, only the working half arrives at the output hybrid, which splits it again: half to the output, half to its terminated isolated port. 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4, i.e. −6 dB. The amplifier still works, at reduced power: graceful degradation.
